title: Neural Networks and Neural Language Models
oneLiner: Build a neural network from one tiny unit, use it to predict the next word, and see how that idea grows into today's large language models.

what.html:
A neural network is layers of simple units. Each unit multiplies its inputs by weights, adds them up, and passes the total through a squashing function. Stack enough of them and train the weights on examples, and the network can classify reviews or predict the next word of a sentence.

Everyday versionThink of a panel of judges, each scoring one aspect of a dish; a head judge combines their scores. Training is adjusting how much each judge's opinion counts until the panel agrees with the real verdicts.

why.html:
• Neural language models handle word combinations never seen in training, which counting can't.
  • The same recipe, scaled up, gives large language models and chatbots.
  • Pretrained models can be reused for new tasks with little data.

how.title: One unit
how.html: Weighted sum plus bias, then an activation: with weights [0.2, 0.3, 0.9], bias 0.5 and inputs [0.5, 0.6, 0.1], the sum is 0.87 and the sigmoid output about 0.705.

how.title: Why one layer isn't enough
how.html: One unit draws a single straight line, so it can do AND and OR but never XOR ("one or the other, not both"). Add a hidden layer and XOR becomes easy.

how.title: Layers and softmax
how.html: Each layer feeds the next. The final softmax turns raw scores into probabilities that add to 1: a score of 3.2 among others near 1 gets about 74%.

how.title: Feeding text in
how.html: Turn each word into a vector, then average (or take the maximum of) the vectors so any length of text becomes one fixed-size input. Easy, but word order is lost.

how.title: Predicting the next word
how.html: Look up vectors for the previous few words, pass them through a hidden layer, and softmax over the whole vocabulary. Because "cat" and "dog" get similar vectors, "the dog gets ___" can be predicted as "fed" even if only the cat sentence was seen.

how.title: Learning from mistakes
how.html: The loss is how little probability the right answer got. Each weight moves a small step in the direction that lowers the loss: with prediction 0.7, true answer 1 and input 2, the weight goes up by 0.06.

how.title: Large language models
how.html: Huge next-word predictors you steer with prompts. Give an instruction (zero-shot) or a few worked examples (few-shot) and the model picks up the task without retraining. Watch for confident but false answers.

how.title: Reuse instead of starting over
how.html: Take a model trained on a big related task, freeze most of it, and train only a new final part on your small dataset; then optionally fine-tune more layers gently. A car-image model becomes a truck-image model with far fewer examples.

demo.html: Move z and compare sigmoid, tanh and ReLU. Tick "show slopes" to see why sigmoid and tanh learn slowly when inputs are large: their slopes flatten to almost zero.

example.html:
Solving XOR. Hidden units h₁ = ReLU(x₁ + x₂) and h₂ = ReLU(x₁ + x₂ − 1), output h₁ − 2h₂. Inputs (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) give hidden values (0,0), (1,0), (1,0), (2,1) and outputs 0, 1, 1, 0: exactly XOR.

Supplementary Many language models reuse the same embedding table for reading words in and for scoring words out, which saves memory and often helps.

misunderstandings: Units are simple arithmetic; the analogy is loose.
More layers without activations add power.
Weights don't change; examples sit in the prompt.
Very different source data can hurt.
takeaways: Unit: z = w·x + b, then sigmoid/tanh/ReLU.
XOR needs a hidden layer (not linearly separable).
Neural LMs use embeddings, so they generalise to unseen contexts.
Train by cross-entropy and gradient descent; reuse with prompting, transfer and fine-tuning.
thirty: A unit computes z = w·x + b and y = g(z) (worked z = 0.87, σ ≈ 0.705). Sigmoid and tanh saturate; ReLU = max(0, z) can die. A perceptron does AND (b = −1) and OR (b = 0) but not XOR, which isn't linearly separable; a ReLU hidden layer (W = [[1,1],[1,1]], b = [0,−1], out h₁ − 2h₂) solves it. Feedforward layers compute a = g(Wa + b); softmax gives probabilities (worked 0.738 for z = 3.2). Text classifiers use features or pooled embeddings (mean [1,2], max [2,4]). A feedforward neural LM concatenates embeddings of the previous words, applies a hidden layer and softmax over V, generalising via similar embeddings (cat/dog gets fed). Training minimises cross-entropy by gradient descent and backprop ((ŷ − y)x; worked +0.06). LLMs are scaled neural LMs used via prompts (zero-/few-shot in-context learning) with hallucination risk; transfer learning and fine-tuning adapt pretrained models.
